I went into this game with pretty high expectations, and somehow it still blew me away. It gives you everything you’d want from a cyberpunk hacking experience without becoming overly abstract or drowning you in technical details. Once you get the hang of the basics, you genuinely feel like the biggest badass hacker on the net. The programs and ICEs were cool, well designed and really captured that Android Netrunner vibe. The writing and story kept me hooked all the way to the end. My only complaint is that some choices had consequences that felt a little too harsh and permanent, and that a few side decisions could have had a bit more payoff. Even so, I loved every single second I spent playing this game. Also, bonus points for the European setting.

Given its a hacking strategy game I super do not agree or enjoy:
- You never see your enemy, you trip into them or guess where they might be (and suffer if your wrong)
- You cannot re-plan missions
- You are not provided enough information ahead of time to know which programs to take along

If these terrible design decisions had been mitigated or provided as optional, we'd have a great game here. I guess the intent is you are to go in with your wits and the tools you have and hope for the best but without any real agency, your just tripping through landmines. Failing forward isn't very fun; it sounds a lot like life.

Wow this is wild

- You literally cannot see ICE before running into them or rolling the dice and using sniffer (maybe your right, maybe your wrong, but you can't use it again for a bit)
- It is in no way obvious that I can restart a mission; I learned outside of the game that I can restart a mission while in the mission but I cannot re-plan (choose better set of programs), which is what I said
- SOME network details are given in advance, not everything as I'd like; how do I reroll and try again?

Look your game isn't for me. I'm not lying or making things up, I have no reason to, the design choices aren't very good from my point of view.
reviews.developer_response:
- Enemy sysops are clearly visible on the network, so claiming they can’t be seen is inaccurate.
- Missions can be easily restarted or adjusted, so it’s not correct to say you’re locked into a plan.
- Network details are given in advance, and even if you bring the wrong deck, you can simply reroll and try again.


Since you've expanded on your points:

- You mentioned enemies, not ICE. But discovering what's actually on the network (whether through the right tools or your own deduction) is part of the core gameplay. If everything were handed to you upfront, what would be left to figure out? This is a role-playing game with dice mechanics, and some of the most celebrated titles, like Baldur's Gate 3, thrive on that exact balance. Mastery in Midnight Protocol comes from learning how to bend those odds in your favor-there are plenty of ways to take control if you play smart.

- And again, that information is available to you. If your loadout isn't ideal, rerolling you adjust your programs and try again-so the idea that you're stuck with a bad setup just doesn't really apply.

Midnight Protocol is a nice little puzzle game. Gameplay itself is interesting mostly for its terminal-like, keyboard only interface. While there are lots of options in the core loop of picking tools and hacking servers, I mostly found myself sticking to the default tools. 
The story about a group of hackers uncovering, sharing and protecting corporate secrets as well as their own enhances the gameplay and made me do more than one side quest to right a wrong.
I really liked the level of variation in the puzzels themselves, with surprise "boss" ICE, fitting illustrations and special effects in the story missions.
Recommended.

This game is an amazing, one-of-a-kind experience. Its very specific but undeniably cool visual presentation, combined with a gripping story full of intrigue and truly unique gameplay, creates an immersive experience that really drew me in.
I also loved how, throughout the game, you constantly feel in control of your experience. From how you build your cyberdeck and choose your program suite to the "color of the hat" your hacker wears, so to speak, and the decisions you make along the way, everything feels meaningful and often has impactful consequences.
Even though some missions were a bit rougher around the edges and required either a very specific approach or a bit of help from the RNG, most of them were very well designed and the gameplay never felt stale.

All in all, it was an amazing ride that I’d highly recommend to anyone with a soft spot for thrillers with a dash of cyberpunk and sci-fi.

Midnight Protocol, developed by LuGus Studios and published by Iceberg Interactive, is a masterfully constructed cyberpunk hacking RPG that forgoes the flashy aesthetics of most games in its genre in favor of tension, intellect, and immersion. It tells the story of a hacker known as Data, who is drawn back into the digital underworld after being doxxed and exposed. The narrative unfolds through encrypted emails, terse chat messages, and system logs, building a world of espionage, distrust, and digital warfare without ever showing a single human face. The game’s story is deeply personal, portraying the isolation and moral grayness of living behind the screen, where every keystroke carries risk and consequence. What begins as a simple act of self-defense quickly evolves into a web of political intrigue, corporate corruption, and cyber rebellion, all told through the restrained, text-based aesthetic of a command-line interface.

The most striking element of Midnight Protocol is its complete commitment to its design philosophy. Every action is performed through the keyboard—no mouse, no icons, just commands typed into a digital terminal. This approach is not merely a stylistic choice but a fundamental part of the experience. It places the player directly in the mindset of a hacker, forcing you to think in terms of efficiency, logic, and spatial reasoning. Networks are depicted as interconnected nodes, each representing firewalls, data caches, security systems, or hidden traps. Your goal varies from mission to mission: infiltrate corporate systems, extract sensitive data, disable rival programs, or manipulate information to your advantage. Each network functions as a puzzle, requiring you to manage limited resources, stay ahead of traces, and decide how far you can push before the system locks you out. Every move carries tension, and the thrill of narrowly escaping detection provides a constant pulse of adrenaline.

What makes these mechanics so engrossing is how they combine strategic planning with improvisation. Each mission feels like a high-stakes chess match played against invisible opponents. You have a library of programs at your disposal—some for stealth, others for brute-force attacks—and choosing the right combination is crucial. The trace system, which measures how close the authorities are to locating you, ensures that every decision feels urgent. Some players might find the reliance on randomness in the trace and detection mechanics slightly frustrating, as even well-planned strategies can fall apart under bad luck. Yet, this unpredictability mirrors the nature of hacking itself—controlled chaos within an unstable system. As your reputation grows and your alignment shifts between white-hat idealism, gray-hat pragmatism, and black-hat ruthlessness, the missions, tools, and story outcomes evolve to reflect your choices. This morality system adds replayability and depth, as it allows players to craft a hacker identity that aligns with their philosophy.

The game’s progression system is intricately tied to its tone of calculated mastery. Through black markets and secret contacts, you acquire new software, upgrade existing tools, and refine your build into a precise digital arsenal. Different playstyles emerge naturally—one player may rely on stealth programs to bypass ICE unnoticed, while another might embrace aggressive, virus-based attacks to dismantle defenses entirely. The learning curve is smooth but demanding, gradually pushing players toward mastery without resorting to handholding. It’s the kind of game that rewards patience and experimentation; every failure is a lesson in systems thinking. The world expands organically through your own initiative: new missions arrive via encrypted emails, hidden coordinates, or anonymous requests. Even the mundane act of checking your in-game inbox feels immersive, as if you are living within a network of digital conspiracies.

Visually, Midnight Protocol is minimalist yet elegant. The interface is clean, the color palette subdued but purposeful—shades of neon blue, black, and red evoke the cold pulse of cyberspace. Despite its simplicity, the design feels immersive, capturing the essence of a digital battlefield through pure abstraction. Every flicker of light and distortion effect contributes to the illusion that you are operating from the edge of legality. The sound design amplifies this immersion with sharp beeps, data pulses, and the low hum of electronic machinery that underscore each command you enter. There is no voice acting or cinematic interlude, but this absence enhances the sense of isolation and authenticity. You are a ghost in the network, unseen and unheard, communicating only through code and action.

The pacing of Midnight Protocol is deliberate, structured around cycles of tension and relief. Missions can be completed in short bursts, yet each one feels meaningful. There are no filler objectives; everything you do contributes to the unraveling of the narrative or your personal evolution as a hacker. While the game never overstays its welcome, some players may wish for a broader scope or more diverse mission environments. The story’s intimate scale, however, fits the tone—this is not about saving the world but about surviving it, carving your path through the static and deceit of a system that’s stacked against you. The writing is terse and precise, and though the characters are only ever seen through text, they feel real, shaped by ideology and consequence rather than cliché.

Midnight Protocol succeeds because it understands exactly what it wants to be—a cerebral, atmospheric strategy game that thrives on immersion, tension, and mechanical purity. It captures the loneliness and allure of the digital frontier, where information is power and morality is fluid. Its stripped-down design and keyboard-driven gameplay make it a niche experience, but within that niche lies something exceptional: a game that makes you feel like a real hacker, navigating systems not through spectacle, but through intellect. It’s a rare experience that balances narrative intrigue with strategic complexity, one that demands attention and rewards mastery. For those who crave precision, immersion, and the thrill of the unknown, Midnight Protocol is a digital labyrinth worth exploring line by line, command by command.

I was having a great time until the "SysOp" gameplay showed up. I didn't understand what other reviewers meant by "like Chess" until then. This isn't really a puzzle or hacking game like I thought it was, it's a board game. That should be in giant letters at the top of the store listing. BOARD GAME. It's not about solving the map, it's about outplaying an AI. You are essentially moving your queen around the board to different squares while trying to avoid opposing pieces that are coming for your piece. This system shows up 6 hours in, after you've already spent your time with the game as a puzzle game, without the "SysOp" stuff. That was an extremely engaging me\ntal exercise in figuring out how to beat the level. The SysOp now becomes how to beat an opponent, and that is less compelling to me as a game. Unfortunately this game altering mechanism doesnt show up until well after the refund period.

Make crystal clear you want to play a CHESS style board game before you buy this. It's well made and polished, but it's not a puzzle or mystery or "hacking" game. Ultimately it isn't for me, and I'm bummed it's not closer to what the store listing makes it out to be. I think if the developer had better set expectations going in I would have a better impression.

Wow, this was absolutely amazing. Yes, it is a bit hard to categorize -- it's more or less a Turn Based Strategy game with RPG elements and a strong story, completely immersed in the "hacking" theme. Do not expect a hacking sim, this is completely "gamefied", but that is exactly what makes it fun.

It starts a bit slow, but once you start to pick up upgrades, you start to think about the choices you must make (what software and hardware to pick for each assignment, for example). It isn't incredibly hard, but it will make you think if you want the best outcomes of all missions. And there are some "secret sidequests" which aren't too hard to find, just make sure you explore the game at your leisure.

But the good gameplay is there to support an amazing story; some of the story beats are really memorable, and expertly presented.

Now, do know the game is played with keyboard only (not even mouse). This is a stylistic choice which makes complete sense in the context of the game. And it **really** works, helping immensely with the illusion you are hacking something.

I run across very few bugs near the end of the game, but they were easily sidestepped. Very recommended, 92/100.

Basically, it's an RPG with turn-based tactical combat and a hackers-themed story with a great interface. The latter may be a point of contention for many — but I, personally, have great affinity for any developer who makes their game playable on keyboard alone (carpal tunnel syndrome is an issue for me). Here, keyboard is the only options, and you'll have to type commands or hotkeys for everything. To me, this adds a lot to the atmosphere and the feel of game. It's a Hollywood-esque take on "hacking" vibe-wise but at same time it's moderately deep from the perspective of tactics and deck-building. So, if something like Duskers and Hacknet is your thing, you're going to enjoy this game a lot. Grabbed during the sale for 5-6 bucks, it's a steal.

Really neat "hacking" game - or more accurately - a cyberpunk-themed puzzle game. It's not quite at the level of the alltime classic, Uplink, but it's really really good. The missions themselves have numerous options that are integrated organically into what you can do. For example, you might be investigating someone's home network and stumble across their bank savings, and you'll have different outcomes based on if you leave it untouched or not.

The developers advertised it on Netrunner adjacent boards. Unfortunately, that's as far as the Netrunner elements go.

You're playing a computer hacker (aka: "Runner" which isn't the term here, so not Netrunner releated) breaking into systems to figure out what has gone on since you were released from jail. Mayhem and hacking ensues.

But the thing is: For all the talk about being Netrunner inspired... it doesn't work. Both you and the AI/SysOp have two actions a turn (compared to Netrunners' 4 Runner 3 SysOp actions a turn). This would be fine... [b][i]IF[/i] the gameplay wasn't timed with the "trace" mechanic[/b] (unlike Netrunners, you can't remove it and you can't buy over the SysOp/Corp to bounce it/avoid the trace).

So you're racing against the clock, facecheck (slam into an ICE defense) and... get fucked over massively in terms of the timer/trace raising in addition to losing an action to where you can't course correct same turn. This means you'll get "trace++" 2+ traces in addition to the end turn trace (which if some ICE is hit, turns off your "cloak" function to try to prevent/stop the trace from increasing, say HELLO to 2-3+ traces off a faceslam).

[i]This is where the game becomes unfun[/i] and if I didn't run into the above review, I would've quit instead of finding the "turn the trace mechanic off" and as the review states: That makes the game somewhat boring because you're [i]turning off an anxiety/timer mechanic[/i] but after a certain point you're like "ok, I'm screwed five ways, why have a sixth?"

Interesting story to go through, but honestly: No, not worth the money. Check the demo out, if you're able to put up with the bad design (needed some more passes to be a bit more fair on the players), go for it. But honestly? I can't recommend it.

Hopefully NetSpectre gives me the Netrunner-a-like I want, but I'm kind of doubting it.

Slay the Spire is pretty much the only one that comes close and even THAT isn't going for Netrunner, but took elements from it.

...My search continues...

[h1]Rating:4/10[/h1]
[b]Completion difficulty:4/10[/b]
Not gonna lie, I just really didn't mesh well with this one. I couldn't quite tell you why, but it all felt so weird and unsatisfying for me. Some levels felt impossible if the RNG wasn't in your favor, or you came in with the wrong toolset (which, you can't always know what toolset to use.) Maybe I'm just bad at the game though.

Midnight Protocol is rich in ambience, in intrigue, in tangled relationships of regret and camaraderie confidently conveyed in nothing more than text, and in more than its fair share of ingenuity.

It's also, unfortunately, like playing chess with only five pieces against a kid who can, at any time, go "yeah no but I had this super power set up HERE, right, all along I had this set up I did, and that means you can't get my guy and, uh, and, um, and and and WHOOOAAA EARTHQUAKE FLIPPED THE BOOOOARD"

You, master hacker that you are, are allowed to do two - count 'em - two succulent and juicy things per turn, and have to sulkily type out 'end' to end your turn thereafter. The goal is to make the most of limited resources against a seemingly unassailable adversary through deft moves and cunning. So far, so hacking-mentality - applaudable.

Yet the execution just doesn't quite make it. Effective red-teaming is about having recon good to go in advance against your target, which you never have in Midnight Protocol - and which costs you precious scant actions per turn to execute in the field instead. The jaws close on you all the while, unless you turn off the Trace mechanic altogether in the game options, and then you're just left with slowly hopping two-by-two across the board poking at things and slowly slurping up cash.

The plot is compelling, rich in injustices and laced with what-ifs, and I wanted to push through and see more of it. Unfortunately, there's a fair bit of padding in the early game that killed the momentum for me. I get it's good to establish characters, lay down rules and playstyles etc., but it'd be so much more exciting for these tidbits to come through organically while enjoying unravelling the story.

A shame, as there's a lot of cool-factor to the whole affair - it just isn't that fun to play.
Enjoyed the tactical sense of this game. The visuals were awesome and the puzzles were fun to get through.

Midnight Protocol is the the best "RPG Hacking game" to date. It's turn-based strategy and interactive story is very engaging. It also has cute references, the in-game tool "hashrat" being my favorite example.

The biggest criticism of this game is that some of the random elements can mess up a mission, but if you go into the game with the mindset that you will fail and learn from the experience, then I'm sure that you will enjoy the experience.

Midnight Protocol is a desktop/hacking sim, and like all of these games, has nothing to do with actual hacking and is utterly unrealistic.  So this is just a strategy (turn based or realtime, you choose) game where you plug away controlling nodes or whatever.  The game does work but it's needlessly convoluted.  I guess to illustrate this, it takes 1/10th the time to learn how to play an RTS like Command & Conquer for 10x the rewarding gameplay.  And even though it's only a 2D game, C&C also has better graphics than this. 

The game design is somewhat flawed in some ways, with a reliance on procgen and RNG that can make or break each challenge. But mostly the game falls flat hard on a very weak and amateurish technical and visual presentation, and sloppy, and in some ways offensive interface design. 

On the upside, the game does feature customisable controls and resolution, so at least some of the basic, minimum requirements have been met.  Unfortunately there's a number of other technical defects and shortcomings which contribute to the game being difficult to recommend to gamers.

The game features lazy minimalist/untextured low-polygon "retro" assets and visuals, making this look like a barely functional 3D game from the early 1990s.  The lack of textures is a method that lazy devs often use to disguise their lack of talent/interest in doing the graphics properly and trying to disguise it under the name of "art", or "We made it look bad on purpose", which really isn't something gamers should have to put up with.  It's unclear why the developers weren't willing to arrange high quality, high polygon count contemporary assets and high resolution textures for the game.  It looks bad as a result of their decisions, and that's just another reason to avoid it.

To make matters worse, there's no mouse input, despite this being sold on PC as if it were a PC game.  This is unacceptable and somewhat insulting.  I know this is on purpose to make it seem like some kind of cool "hacker" game but this is annoying. Don't do this.  No developer should ever dictate to gamers how a game is to be played, ever. 

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

Midnight Protocol didn't appeal much to the people who own a copy of the game, either.  It has achievements, and they show us a very clear picture that the game didn't really capture any interest from gamers.  The most commonly and easily attained achievement is for finishing the tutorial, trivial to get, but less than 39 percent of players bothered to get that far before uninstalling the game.  Hardly a success story, gamers just weren't all that interested in the game.

So, should you buy this game?  Is this one of the best of the 100,000+ games on Steam?

Midnight Protocol has the laughable, eye-watering price of $15 USD, for which you could easily get any number of older AAA games.  Given the defects and quality issues with the game, coupled with the unrealistic price, this is impossible to recommend.

For comparison, the $15 asking price for this game could get you games like "Mass Effect Andromeda", "Project Zomboid" or "Stellaris".  Quality, professionally made games like those are frequently on sale cheaper than this.

reviews.review: Really great game for cyberpunk fans as well as anybody that likes puzzles. The keyboard controls may put some people off, but you get used to them quick and in return you get a really cleverly constructed game with a really fun story.
Had a ton of fun with it, and really enjoyed the feeling, but then percentage based chance made the game a tossup. Refunded.

Very fun and immersive, I kept coming back to try new strategies on levels I struggled with. Story was not what I expected. Really hoping they make a sequel as there are lots of cool design choices. Just beat it and tempted to immediately replay!

Do you know anything about hackers? 
Can you jam with the console cowboys in cyberspace? 
Ever read Neuromancer? 
Ever experienced the new wave, next wave, dream wave, or cyberpunk?
Very cool hacker game! Would DEFINITELY recommend it!

Let's start with the positives. The visuals are very good, very "hackery" and just very pleasing to look at. It's also keyboard only, which further enhances the immersion.

And this is about it when it comes to the positives.

It's almost fundamentally not a hacking game. You could easily swap out all of the "commands" for just fantasy spells. You're not breaking into systems to gather information, to gather passwords to use on other networks (i.e. puzzle solving). Each "mission" is fundamentally independent. You're there to get money (or complete objectives for the story) and then leave.

There's also the weird RNG aspect of the game. Your "attacks" against "firewalls" can "crit". Not to mention, how many actions waste your action points, which is also complemented by how few turns you actually from being caught.

The developer has a solid foundation to creating an interesting hacking game. But if they're going to do a RNG/RPG turn-based game, then stick to fantasy/sci-fi instead.
Super fun hacker game. If you like Shadow run as a decker, this is the game for you.
Simple, yet great turn based game with an original concept, great music, aesthetics, plot and overall vibe!
Sometimes I think the Trace Meter goes up just to spite me.
reviews.developer_response: Various strategies and decks can be crafted to counteract the tracing element of a hack, it all depends on your choices and playstyle. Take control of the network, not the other way around ;)

reviews.review:
If you like [i]Hollywood Hacking[/i], you're going to love this one!

The hacking mechanic is turn-based, where you have to decide how to use your two action points, either by moving around the "network" you're hacking, or using a "program". Effectiveness of the programs depends on how many "slices" of power from your hardware you allocate to each one (re-allocating slices doesn't consume actions).

When your turn is done, your opponents (AIs, Sysops, other hackers...) will move following almost the same rules (for example, Sysadmins are not affected by the booby traps laid out in the network)

Your time on the network (the number of turns) is limited by a "Trace" that ends up aborting your mission.

Most of the story is conveyed by written email/chats. There are some moments that will require you to type an email or a chat message to progress. Those can be "hacker-typed" (quite fun, to be honest) or skipped by pressing TAB.

The background is a story about identity, revenge and AI. Very cool!

Nice idea but suffers from missions that are far too specific with not enough information to create a proper loadout and worse those missions can not be retried without crashing out of the game.  Shame because I was interested in the story but multiple failed missions due to this or RNG just makes you not want to progress,

Can't replay failed missions. You are limited to 5 "tools" in your load out, and sometimes don't realize you need a specific type of tool until you're in the mission. Too bad. You are stuck and you will fail and then you will be locked out from trying. I'm all for a difficult challenge, but if it locks you out from the story progressing, it stops being fun and just becomes frustrating.
reviews.developer_response: The game never locks you out of story progression. In fact, "failing" a mission is considered a valid narrative outcome that could potentially unlock other storylines. The game also gives hints about what you will encounter on a network, and you can, at all times, reload a mission within a network with a new loadout. Depending on your unlocks and choices, you are not limited to 5 programs. Last but not least, you can set a different difficulty level in-game.

reviews.review: Gameplay wise it is very much like DnD with a cyber twist. A touching story with player choice driven narrative, this game is amazingly well made. The highest discount was seen at -50%, however, considering the high quality of the game, you have all the reason to purchase it at -20%.

pretty awesome game if your in to the concept of typing based games, hacking, and things like that. I've never played a game like this before and I thought I would find it boring even, needless to say, these seven hours I have in it will be the first of many more to come. I'd say if you're interested in this concept 100% try it out. It's not worth missing this gem because of a bad review.

I'm surprised this game doesn't get more attention!  Excellent, if not perfect, indie game.  Strategy game that gives you the feeling of being an elite hacker.  Punches above it's weight in terms of presentation.  Highly recommend.
Underrated, I highly recommend this game

I got bored with this pretty quickly. The problem is that the hacking game is pretty simplistic, and doesn't require any strategy. Sniff for security barriers, advance if they're not there, attack them if they are. Sometimes  you'll just spend several turns waiting for the barrier to come down. I never felt like I was doing anything that required any thought.

Maybe that improves as the game advances, but if I'm still twiddling my thumbs at the 3 hour mark, it's time to move on to something more interesting.
reviews.developer_response: If you've only been playing for 3 hours, chances are you're still in the game's introductory phase. With over 20 hours of content, you'll soon discover the need to swiftly adjust your initial strategy.

reviews.review: It's a great strategy game that hearkens back to the hacker simulators of the early 2000s.

Really enjoyed this, both the puzzles and the story and the hacking aesthetic. Fundamentally, the elevator pitch of this game is "Mankind Divided if it was collapsed to its hacking mini-game (but turn-based)". If you are a fan of turn-based tactics and H A C K I N G (or sci-fi in general), then I would strongly recommend this game.

+ The puzzle/tactics aspect is fun and varied. You continuously gain new abilities, but they complement, rather than replace, the ones you already have.
+ The missions are quite diverse and varied too, requiring you to shuffle your build from mission to mission.
+ The story is a very solid sci-fi tale with a decent amount of world-building and side-quests. So even though the main quest is always flashing on your screen, you can get at least somewhat immersed in the world and its history on the side, which I greatly appreciate.
+ There is a fair bit of non-linearity, with the intent being that "any choice you make is valid", which lends a lot of credibility to the narrative, and makes the choices you make that much more meaningful (as opposed to "do you accept a generic sidequest? y/n"). At least early on.

- My main complaint would probably be about the slight schizophrenia in game/mission design that the game succumbs to. On the one hand, the game suggests that "any choice is valid", meaning the player is expected to roll with the punches -- you should prepare for any mission the best you can based on the info given to you in advance, and any mission you fail weighs on your consciousness, but the story continues regardless. (For the record, I tried my best to adhere to this philosophy and accept the consequences.) However, about half-way through, the game starts saying "hey, this mission is critical, you can't quit and you can't fail", so if you fail you just start over (with an option to change your loadout). In effect, this means that in most missions from that point onwards, you have no choice but to savescum: first see the mission, learn the layout and the threats, and then equip the optimal loadout. 
I understand the difficulties of mission design and narrative design and all kinds of design that led to this outcome, but as a player, at that point I felt cheated. As a "reviewer", I am not sure what could have been a better way. Leaning all-in on the "everything allowed" approach would've put a very low difficulty ceiling and/or required a *lot* of extra writing. Taking it out completely would greatly harm the immersion the game offers in the first half. So... yeah... It's good but I can't help but wonder if it could've been even better.

- Also 0451 doesn't open any doors, bad cyberpunk game, 2/10. (Or does it? This playthrough took too long...)
This is a puzzle game at heart but it is surrounded by an immersive shell that surprises and delights. Highly recommended for fans of cyberpunk fiction and games that transport you.

One of the best hacking sims I've played. Challenging hacking puzzles, full of atmosphere and loaded with extra features and details, a comprehensive experience. And a story to pull you through it!

Midnight protocol is an interesting hacker RPG with a good plot and a story that reacts to your choices. The game becomes a bit repetitive after 15h or so. Some midgame elements can make the game too easy and less interesting (I had to force myself to stop using my cookie-cutter build and try new things).However, most late-game story missions are very cool and  the game manages to stay interesting until the end. Recommended !
Love this game. Far exceeded my expectations. So much fun!

Midnight Protocol is an excellent dive into 'HACKER CULTURE' a la Cyberpunk. Playing in a future universe, you manipulate an archaic-feeling digital terminal to hack into networks, remove defenses, and save the world from corpo scum. The mechanics are simple - almost exclusively text based - and feel immersive. I felt smug dodging enemy admins, clever when I guessed passwords based on information I'd gathered, and accomplished when I completed missions that had been giving me trouble. It delivers on its promises.

The plot was unexpectedly good, far exceeding my expectations. I understand there are multiple endings as well, though I only played through the once. I enjoyed it a lot. I will say no more for spoiler reasons.

My only critique is that the game feels like a puzzle game, but frequently makes it very difficult to solve the puzzle without resetting the level. While I don't mind it, many might feel like this is 'save scumming' and I wish there was a better way to resolve not having the right programs to handle a challenge than just resetting. They do minimize you ability to 'cheat' my randomizing many defenses between attempts, but the information gain is still significant at times.

Overall, I would strongly recommend this game. I finished it with 52 hours on the Steam clock, but I believe I left it on overnight. I managed to beat it in a couple of days of dedicated play. For the price, it was a great time!

What an awesome game. As an avid Android:Netrunner player, I really enjoyed how the theme and story fit really together with the mechanics to create a great experience.

The game at it's core is split into two sides.
- the "prep" side where you chat with your contacts, choose what missions you'll accept, and what programs you'll bring.
- the "mission" side, which is an action-economy boardgame where you traverse a network of nodes towards an objective, break / avoid ICE, all while a trace timer counts up to your doom.

With such a solid core system, I would have expected any other developer to just "phone in" the actual level design, and just procedurally generate the missions, but this is not the case here. Instead, every mission is hand crafted, unique in it's own way, and you can really feel the attention to detail and love that was put into each experience, which is just so refreshing in the current state of gaming that ask you to just to the same thing over and over with minor variations.

[b]On RNG[/b]
Much of the criticism I see in other reviews talks about the "RNG" of tracing and ICE placements, but I have to disagree. Choosing between putting more of your resources into delaying the trace to play it slow and steady versus making the calculated mad dash to the finish is PEAK NETRUNNER. I will say that I started out playing very cautiously, and managing cloak slices while waiting for dagger to break through felt tedious. By the end, I had freed myself from my safe shell and embraced the run, preferring to sidestep, bypass, or just facetank ICE instead.

[b]On Playstyle[/b]
On a similar note, I do think that this game heavily encourages you to use different programs due to adapt to different the missions, so if you're a stickler for your favourite deck setup, you may find like you're trying to brute force your square solution into the circular hole. There's a bit of information revealed before you start a mission, letting you know if you should even bring a specific type of program. From there, you bring your favourite set and hope for the best. 

Should you fail, the game lets you quickly restart, or even backout to the pre-mission deck configuration step. A few of the other reviews find a way to complain about this, stating that "the game expects you to just lose on your first run, so that you can back out and come back in with perfect 'meta' knowledge", but again I disagree. 
- The initial run is thrilling, in a "discovering the unknown and doing my best with what I've got" way, which again, is PEAK NETRUNNER. I completed most missions with my initial deck configuration.
- The follow up / reconfigured / "meta informed" runs are also satisfying, in a "I am the ultimate runner, witness how I effortlessly defeat your defences" way. I found I preferred to swap to more "informed" setups after failing some of the harder story missions.

[b]Conclusion[/b]
I really recommend this game. It's fun, the mechanics and theme work great together, and the missions are all lovingly crafted and unique. I found myself saying "wow this is so cool" constantly.

I'm glad I stuck with this game long enough to get through my "safe shell" phase of tediously chipping away at ICE and managing cloak slices. While everyone starts out playing safe, it's nice when new programs become available to let you run a little more recklessly.

The pacing of the story is way too slow and the RNG is WAY too harsh. I do not want to replay the same level 8 times because of bad luck. Other than that, the game play becomes repetitive very quickly. Some really cool ideas, but really not worth it unless you just LOVE RNG puzzles.

Highly recommended if you are a fan of the hacking genre and keyboard games. 

The game mechanic is fun and the story is interesting and well paced. You can adjust the difficulty such that you get to simply enjoy the story too.

Tips: if you've got a macro software, set up hotkeys for end turn, reload game, and reload+redeck to save on a bunch of precise keypresses. And make use of the in-game alias command to register typos too, like if you hit a comma instead of a fullstop. I prefer to type move instead of . but I do occasionally typo it to mvoe and sometimes begin typing before the game lets me so i end up with just ve, but using aliases on all these variations means I don't have to backspace everything.

I don't normally write reviews, but considering this gem has only 162 reviews at the time of writing, I kinda have to do it - it just deserves much better visibility.

First thing's first - this is not a hacking game - you don't need any real hacking knowledge and you won't earn any either. It just borrows some general "hacking aesthetic" - you need to uncover secrets that was not supposed to ever go public, unlock new malware on black market that helps you proceed, you consult your fellow hack buddies, get to make some decisions that affect real people outside of the net - all that while combating the threat of being traced. And oh, all that is achieved exclusively by typing commands. Gameplay-wise, I found it pretty fun, but after you unlock some programs that might be a little too OP, the game might become a bit too easy and stale. You can unlock some challenges to make it harder though, but personally I didn't see a point. The game does everything to combat the staleness though - even the most broken combos won't work in every other situation - you have to change your loadout quite often. Also, the production value is on an unreal level - there are quite a lot of special one-time mechanics just for that level.

The main thing that made me glued to the monitor though, was the story. It starts a bit slow, but delivers EXPERTLY. It manages to make you care about your buddies - even though you don't really know much about them - anonymity is a thing in the hacking world after all. It telegraphs certain story points to make you feel like you know what's going to happen and still manages to throw you off. I also really adore how the writers leveraged the fact that it feels like you - the player, in our world - is doing all this nerdy stuff, hacking, emailing and so on - but no spoilers - you'd have to see that for yourself. 

The music though may be the weakest link in the game - it's nice, but I felt like there is only one track playing over and over and over. Even the boss music is a variation of the same track - this is actually pretty nice, because you feel there are some stakes involved. 

Concluding - you should really get the game - it's absolutely worth every penny.
Great game!

Midnight Protocol is a fun, surprisingly expansive hacking game that does an excellent job of balancing tension and difficulty with flexible gameplay and a deep, thoughtful story. This isn't a real-time hacking sim like Uplink or Nethack -- it's a turn-based, more puzzle-oriented game where you're exploring systems while dodging ICE and enemy operators (though like those games, it's controlled 100% by typing). But make no mistake, even with its turn-based nature it still manages to ratchet up the tension as trace meters rise and turn timers tick down.

What I enjoyed was that the wide variety of apps and hardware systems let players approach security systems in multiple ways. For instance, my go-to kit was a slow and steady loadout of high trace security and the "hive" program which grows in power for each infected system node. I would methodically march around systems, infecting everywhere I touched while staying under the radar, until I could hammer away at the ICE security systems with a powerful strike. Thankfully, though, the game forces you to adapt by mixing up security systems and other gameplay elements. I had to toss my approach out the window for levels that had strict turn timers, ditching security for a deck geared around an all-out hacking sprint.

The story is excellent and surprised me with its depth and complexity, including multiple opportunities for player choice and expression. Almost every conversation is strictly via email or chat but by the end the game had crafted multiple fully fleshed-out characters who I was deeply invested in.

I wish more people would play this game. If you're a fan of hacking games, puzzlers, or board games (the gameplay elements seem wonderfully suited for a tabletop edition), I highly recommend it.

So.  Someone took a very graphics oriented strategy / sort of puzzle game and replaced the obvious easy mouse controls  with a lot  of  typing.  If this were the sort of game that looked like an 80's hacker movie then this  would work.  But Midnight Protocol looks more like Tron or Johnny Mnemonic.  And the extra cumbersome type it all out control scheme just does not add to the experience.  It does  rather the opposite.  It fells wrong and it's needlessly slow.  And this is it's selling point?
There are significantly better "hacker" games.  I'd recommend one of them instead.

I was Zero Cool.

Obligatory reference aside, this is a really unique take on tactical games. I really like that there is no mouse and the entire game takes place using the keyboard. The atmosphere of the operating system combined with typing commands really made me feel like I was playing the part of a hacker. The emails received make the game feel surprisingly lifelike for the amount of text the game is made of. There were times I would send an email, go AFK for a bit, come back, and I'd have a response, felt legit. The music and noises all gave me a great vibe that was quite immersive.

I also appreciated that some progression is through actions that are altruistic, selfish, or ambiguous/neutral. The choices I made allowed me to unlock different upgrades, and at times I was making decisions I didn't necessarily agree with just so I could get an unlock, which certainly made me feel some type of way. At times I found myself examining the gray area in actions which were considered selfish. It's okay to steal from this lady's personal savings for this reason but not from her daughter's college fund, so I'll leave that alone. 

I spent around 20-25 hours completing the story, all side missions, and 66% of achievements. I would definitely recommend picking it up if you like tactical games. The game at full price is a steal, but if it's on sale it's a no-brainer. Much respect for the game and the devs. Thank you for making this great and unique game. Keep up the good work!
genuinely such a good game.
excellent hacking game with a great story. unfortunately, i find hacking games to be boring, and this one gets both repetitive and RNG-heavy, but the writing was good enough for me to finish.

A pretty solid game, with a haunting plot and accompanying sound track! Hits that sweet spot for 'hacker' games, where it can make you feel like your exercising skill without being too much like the real thing (I work in infosec, if I want to do real hacking I'll do it in TryHackMe or a bug bounty - it takes ages and is usually boring). A slick presentation, and the keyboard-only interface is really swift to navigate about after a very short learning curve. Good stuff!

Stopped having fun after 2 hours and do not intend to continue :( Game seems okay but I could not figure out which tools to use correctly to finish levels. You can cheat the system by keep restarting but I do not find that approach fun. I try to do my best first try every level and roll with the punches but like I said I could not figure out a good way to do it. 

You can bring 5 tools with you to every level, and there is a trace counter increasing at every step where the maximum trace results in a failure. Then you need to bring an item called cloak to decrease the probability of gaining trace, then because you need to use cloak you cannot use some other items so they are gone. If there are blockers in your way you need the sniffer to find them and dagger to destroy them while hoping cloak does its work. This is already 3 out of 5 items fixed for you. I don't know, I do not get it and I do not find it fun so I do not recommend the game.

Just a big buggy waste of time, nothing special here. The strategy gameplay is very limited and the "story" in between each mission is frustrating to navigate how to unlock the next mission. Also technical issues such as bugs that softlock forcing a restart, and audio coming through even though master volume is set to 0. [strike]The "Finish Act 1" achievement is less than 10% of players which shows the retention of interest here[/strike] without going into detail about the positives and negatives of this game.
